Learning analytics team project

What student behavior can and cannot predict

We studied whether behavior inside Carnegie Learning’s MATHia platform could predict what students learned and how they experienced learning.

The clear result

Platform behavior carried a strong signal for later math performance.

The practical insight

The timing of a hint click separated strategic review from a deeper difficulty getting started.

About 75%

of the differences in later math performance appeared in the behavioral signal.

Two patterns

of immediate hint use required different forms of support.

Three ideas

turned the observation into changes for the learning experience.

Strong resultAbout 75%

Behavior carried a useful signal for later math performance

Practice performance, mastery progress, engagement, errors, and help use together captured roughly three quarters of the differences in later math performance.

Most useful evidenceAnswers, errors, mastery, progress, and help use

Use boundary: motivation and metacognition were not reliable enough for conclusions about an individual student.

A hint click was not a single story

Opening a question hint quickly could look like low persistence. Later performance showed that timing and context changed what the action meant.

Pattern one

Quick hints supported recall but not always transfer

These students often performed well on short quizzes. For concept questions, a hint could refresh a definition, term, or principle while it was still relevant.

The advantage faded on broader assessments.

When a problem required several reasoning steps or independent application, recall was not enough. The student needed practice applying the concept without the same scaffold.

Support needMore independent application and retrieval practice
Pattern two

A hint before any attempt signaled difficulty starting

These students performed below average on both short quizzes and larger exams.

The timing changed the meaning of the click.

They may not have known how to enter the problem at all. Foundational review, teacher follow up, and guidance toward the first productive step were more appropriate.

Support needBasic understanding and help choosing a starting point

Three product ideas generated from the observation

01 Progressive hints

Offer a simple reminder first, then reveal guidance one step at a time.

02 Reflection time

Add a short pause between hints so students can attempt the next step themselves.

03 Concept resurfacing

Bring the same concept back later through a different problem and test independent retrieval.

Enough method to trust the result

Each outcome received its own model and was checked against student records it had not seen before.

Behavior

We summarized practice, progress, persistence, errors, and hint timing for each student.

Independent check

Validation tested whether the patterns held beyond the records used to build the model.

Stability

Repeated checks showed that math results held up while the psychological outcomes remained noisy.

Responsible use

The strength of the evidence should determine how a prediction is used.

Use math predictions as an early signal

The model could help educators notice students who may need support, while keeping the teacher in the decision.

Do not label internal states from clicks

Motivation and metacognition need richer evidence such as brief student reflection, affective measures, and teacher context.
